questions.q: What is the default join type of DataFrame.join() when `how` is not given?

options.t: left, keeping every row of the left DataFrame even without a match
options.why: The default is inner.

options.t: inner
full outer, keeping unmatched rows from both sides with nulls
options.why: The default is inner.

options.t: cross, pairing every row with every row of the other side
options.why: The default is inner.

questions.explain: df.join(other, on, how): how defaults to inner, and may be inner, cross, outer/full, left, right, semi/left_semi or anti/left_anti.

questions.q: Orders must be joined to order lines on both `order_id` and `line_no`. How is a multi-key join written with DataFrame.join()?

options.t: Two joins in a row, one per key, then a distinct to remove the extra rows
options.why: Pass both keys to a single join; on accepts a list of columns.

options.t: A cross join followed by a filter on both keys
options.why: That works but is wasteful; a multi-key join passes a list to on.

options.t: orders.join(lines, on=["order_id", "line_no"])
orders.join(lines, on="order_id" + "line_no"), concatenating the names
options.why: That would look for a single column named order_idline_no.

questions.explain: The on parameter can be a list of column names for a multi-key join.

questions.q: A reconciliation check must list orders that have no matching payment. Which join type returns exactly those orders, with only the orders' columns?

options.t: left_anti
left_semi, which keeps left rows that have a match on the right
options.why: A semi join keeps orders that do have a payment.

options.t: full outer, then a filter for nulls on both sides of the join
options.why: That returns rows from both sides; an anti join returns just the unmatched left rows.

options.t: inner, then subtracting the result from the orders table afterwards
options.why: An anti join does this directly.

questions.explain: An anti (left_anti) join keeps rows of the left side that have no match on the right, without adding columns from the right.

questions.q: Which join type keeps the left rows that do have a match, without adding any columns from the right side?

options.t: inner, which also adds the right side's columns to every row
options.why: An inner join adds the right side's columns; a semi join doesn't.

options.t: left, which also keeps left rows that have no match at all
options.why: A left join keeps unmatched rows too and adds right columns.

options.t: left_semi
cross, which pairs every left row with every right row
options.why: A cross join pairs everything; it doesn't filter by match.

questions.explain: A semi join keeps rows of the left side that have a match, without adding columns: 'orders that have a payment'.

questions.q: A large fact table is joined to a small dimension table. Which hint asks Spark to send the small table to every executor so the large one isn't shuffled?

options.t: /*+ SHUFFLE_HASH(dim) */, which hashes both sides across the cluster
options.why: SHUFFLE_HASH shuffles both sides; BROADCAST sends the small side to every executor.

options.t: /*+ MERGE(dim) */, which requests a sort-merge join on the keys
options.why: MERGE asks for a sort-merge join, which shuffles.

options.t: /*+ REBALANCE */, which evens out the output partitions
options.why: REBALANCE addresses skewed output, not join strategy.

options.t: /*+ BROADCAST(dim) */

questions.explain: A broadcast join sends the small table to every executor; hint it with BROADCAST. The join strategy hints in priority order are BROADCAST, MERGE, SHUFFLE_HASH and SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL.

questions.q: Below what size does Apache Spark broadcast a join side automatically, by default?

options.t: 1 MB, the setting's default in Spark 4
options.why: Apache Spark's default spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold is 10 MB.

options.t: 10 MB
100 MB, the setting's default in Spark 4
options.why: Apache Spark's default is 10 MB.

options.t: There is no automatic broadcasting; only hints broadcast
options.why: Spark broadcasts automatically below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold.

questions.explain: spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold is Apache Spark's limit for broadcasting a table to every worker in a join, 10 MB by default; -1 disables broadcasting. Databricks Runtime can set its own defaults.

questions.q: How do you stop Spark from broadcasting any join side automatically?

options.t: Set spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to -1
Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 0 so no broadcast partitions exist
options.why: That setting controls shuffle partitions, not broadcasting.

options.t: Set spark.sql.adaptive.enabled to false, which removes broadcast joins
options.why: AQE can switch to broadcast at run time, but the threshold setting disables automatic broadcasting.

options.t: Add the /*+ MERGE */ hint to every query in the workspace
options.why: Hints act per query; the threshold of -1 disables automatic broadcasting.

questions.explain: Setting spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to -1 disables automatic broadcasting.

questions.q: DataFrame a holds x = 1, 2 and DataFrame b holds x = 2, 3. How many rows does a.union(b) return?

options.t: 3, because union removes the duplicate 2 like SQL UNION does
options.why: DataFrame union keeps duplicates, like SQL UNION ALL.

options.t: 2, because only rows found in both are kept by a union
options.why: That would be an intersection.

options.t: 1, the row that appears in both DataFrames
options.why: That would be an intersection.

questions.explain: union() and unionAll() keep duplicates (no automatic deduplication), so the result has 1, 2, 2, 3. Add .distinct() to deduplicate.

questions.q: In SQL, what is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?

options.t: UNION keeps duplicates; UNION ALL removes them
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.t: UNION matches columns by name; UNION ALL by position
options.why: Both match by position; the difference is deduplication.

options.t: UNION works only on Delta tables; UNION ALL works on any table
options.why: The difference is deduplication, not table formats.

options.t: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them

questions.explain: In SQL, UNION (the same as UNION DISTINCT) removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them. DataFrame union() behaves like UNION ALL.

questions.q: Two DataFrames have the same columns in a different order. Which method combines them correctly?

options.t: union(), which lines columns up automatically by their names
options.why: union matches columns by position, so values land in the wrong columns.

options.t: unionByName()
unionAll(), the version of union that checks column names
options.why: unionAll also matches by position.

options.t: join() on all columns, which concatenates the two DataFrames
options.why: A join pairs rows; it doesn't append them.

questions.explain: unionByName() matches columns by name (and with allowMissingColumns=True fills missing columns with null); union() and unionAll() match by position.

questions.q: One DataFrame has an extra column `channel` that the other lacks. Which call appends them and fills the missing column with null?

options.t: a.union(b), which pads any missing columns with null
options.why: union needs the same number of columns and matches by position.

options.t: a.unionAll(b).fillna(None), which adds the column afterwards
options.why: unionAll also matches by position and can't add a column.

options.t: a.join(b, how="outer"), which keeps columns from both sides
options.why: A join pairs rows rather than appending them.

options.t: a.unionByName(b, allowMissingColumns=True)

questions.explain: unionByName with allowMissingColumns=True fills columns missing on one side with null.

questions.q: A column `tags` holds arrays of strings. Which function turns each element into its own row?

options.t: split(tags), which separates the array into rows
options.why: split turns a string into an array; explode turns an array into rows.

options.t: explode(tags)
collect_list(tags), which spreads a list into rows
options.why: collect_list does the opposite: it gathers values into an array.

options.t: flatten(tags), which flattens nested arrays into rows
options.why: flatten merges nested arrays into one array; it doesn't create rows.

questions.explain: explode(col) returns one row per element of an array (or entry of a map).

questions.q: A dashboard needs a cheap estimate of distinct customers over billions of rows. Which function fits?

options.t: approx_count_distinct(customer_id)
count(customer_id), which counts each customer once
options.why: count counts non-null values, not distinct ones.

options.t: countDistinct over a window, which samples the data first
options.why: approx_count_distinct is the cheap estimate.

options.t: summary(), which returns the distinct count of every column
options.why: summary gives count, mean, stddev, min, quartiles and max, not distinct counts.

questions.explain: approx_count_distinct(col, rsd=0.05) estimates a distinct count cheaply; the default maximum relative standard deviation is 0.05.

questions.q: approx_count_distinct accepts a maximum relative standard deviation, rsd. What does the documentation say happens below rsd = 0.01?

options.t: It returns an exact count, so it is always preferred over count_distinct
options.why: The documentation says count_distinct is more efficient below 0.01.

options.t: It raises an error, because 0.01 is the minimum allowed value
options.why: The documentation points to count_distinct, not an error.

options.t: count_distinct is more efficient
It switches to sampling one percent of the rows to save time
options.why: Below 0.01, the exact count_distinct is the more efficient choice.

questions.explain: The default rsd is 0.05; for rsd below 0.01, count_distinct is more efficient.

questions.q: Which statistics does DataFrame.summary() compute by default?

options.t: Only the row count and number of nulls for each column
options.why: summary computes more than counts.

options.t: Distinct counts and the most frequent value of each column
options.why: Those aren't among summary's default statistics.

options.t: Count, mean, stddev, min, approximate quartiles and max
The column's data type, nullability and comment from the schema
options.why: That is schema information, not statistics.

questions.explain: summary() computes count, mean, stddev, min, approximate 25/50/75% percentiles and max by default.

questions.q: A silver table must keep one row per `order_id`. Which call removes duplicates on that column only?

options.t: df.distinct(), which keeps one row per first column
options.why: distinct compares every column, not just order_id.

options.t: df.dropDuplicates(["order_id"])
df.groupBy("order_id").count(), which keeps each order's latest row
options.why: That returns counts per order, not the rows.

options.t: df.union(df), which merges duplicate rows together
options.why: union keeps duplicates; it doesn't remove them.

questions.explain: dropDuplicates(subset) removes duplicate rows, optionally on chosen columns.

questions.q: dropDuplicates is applied to a stream. What must bound the state it keeps across micro-batches?

options.t: A rate limit such as maxFilesPerTrigger on the source
options.why: Rate limits size batches; a watermark bounds deduplication state.

options.t: The complete output mode, which clears state every trigger
options.why: Complete mode doesn't clear state; a watermark bounds it.

options.t: A watermark
Nothing: streaming deduplication keeps no state at all
options.why: On a stream it keeps state across triggers.

questions.explain: On a stream, dropDuplicates keeps state across triggers, bounded by withWatermark().

questions.q: Which work belongs in the silver layer of a medallion architecture?

options.t: Cleaning, deduplication, type casting, null handling and quality checks
Keeping the source data unchanged, as it arrived, for audit and replay
options.why: That is bronze.

options.t: Aggregating sales by day for executive dashboards and reports
options.why: Business aggregates belong in gold.

options.t: Nothing; silver is optional and only copies bronze for safekeeping
options.why: Silver is where data is validated and conformed.

questions.explain: Silver does cleaning, deduplication, normalisation, null handling, type casting, joins, schema enforcement and evolution, late data handling and quality checks, keeping a validated non-aggregated version of each record.

questions.q: Which describes the gold layer?

options.t: Raw data appended as it arrived, with provenance metadata attached
options.why: That is bronze.

options.t: Validated, deduplicated records kept one per source event
options.why: That is silver.

options.t: A staging area for files before they become tables in the lake
options.why: Files land in volumes; gold is business-ready tables.

options.t: Dimensional models and aggregates for the business

questions.explain: Gold holds dimensional models and aggregates aligned to business needs, such as a materialized view behind a dashboard.

questions.q: How does Databricks describe the medallion architecture?

options.t: A Unity Catalog feature that must be switched on for each catalog
options.why: It is a data design pattern, not a feature.

options.t: A recommended best practice, but not a requirement
A requirement for any table written by a Lakeflow pipeline
options.why: Databricks calls it a recommended best practice, not a requirement.

options.t: A naming rule enforced on schemas called bronze, silver and gold
options.why: The layers are a convention, not an enforced rule.

questions.explain: The medallion architecture (also multi-hop) is a data design pattern of layers that improve quality step by step; Databricks calls it a recommended best practice but not a requirement.

questions.q: How does Databricks suggest reading append-only bronze tables to build silver?

options.t: Mostly with streaming reads
With a full batch reread of bronze every run, to catch any changes
options.why: Databricks suggests streaming reads of append-only bronze, with batch for small dimensions.

options.t: Only through time travel to the previous version of bronze
options.why: Time travel isn't the incremental pattern; streaming reads are.

options.t: By copying bronze files into silver's folder with a file system tool
options.why: Copying files bypasses Delta; silver is built with streaming reads.

questions.explain: Build silver from bronze, mostly with streaming reads of the append-only bronze tables; small dimension tables can be read in batch.

questions.q: What does spark.sql.shuffle.partitions control?

options.t: How many files each Delta table may have before compaction runs
options.why: It sets the number of partitions used when shuffling for joins and aggregations.

options.t: The number of partitions used when shuffling data for joins or aggregations
How many executors the cluster starts with before autoscaling
options.why: It is a partition count, not an executor count.

options.t: How many partitions a Delta table is split into on disk
options.why: It concerns shuffles at query time, not table layout.

questions.explain: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions is 'the number of partitions to use when shuffling data for joins or aggregations', 200 by default in Apache Spark.
